extracted.intended_audience: performers, comedy students, writers, and general readers interested in comedic delivery and humor styles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for performing or recognizing deadpan (dry) humour: the deliberate use of emotional neutrality and specific delivery traits to produce comedy by contrast with absurd content or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate emotional neutrality (definition & purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadpan (dry humour, or dry-wit humour) is the deliberate display of emotional neutrality or no emotion, commonly as a form of comedic delivery, to contrast with the ridiculousness or absurdity of the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The delivery is meant to be blunt, ironic, laconic, or apparently unintentional. Use neutral affect deliberately so the humour arises from the contrast between the content and the performer's lack of visible reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expression and physical stillness
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an expressionless face and minimal physical movement as part of the delivery (e.g., 'playing a role with expressionless face', 'stony expression', 'standing completely still and without a smile').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and exemplary notes: performers like Buster Keaton kept a stony expression and found audiences responded better when he did not smile; T. W. Barrett performed standing completely still and without a smile. Anti-pattern: breaking the expression (smiling, exaggerated gestures) undermines the deadpan effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal delivery characteristics: blunt, ironic, laconic, apparently unintentional
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of speaking in deadpan should be blunt, ironic, laconic, or appear unintentional, enhancing contrast between form and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimal inflection, dry wording, or an apparently offhand comment (a 'throwaway line') so the audience perceives the incongruity. Examples from the page include many TV and film characters who deliver absurd lines in this tone (e.g., Leslie Nielsen post-Airplane!, Bill Murray, John Cleese/Edmund Blackadder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on context and contradiction for humour (audience inference requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The humour often does not exist in the words or delivery alone; the listener must look for humour in the contradiction between words, delivery and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the performer fails to include sufficient context or the audience does not identify the contradiction, the dry humour will likely fall flat. This is a common failure mode explicitly noted: 'Failure to include the context or to identify the contradiction results in the listener finding the dry humour unfunny.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan is a delivery method distinct from content-based categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadpan refers only to the method of delivery rather than to the type or intellectual level of the humour (e.g., it is separate from 'dry humour' as a label for certain comedic content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate deadpan (delivery) with highbrow/egghead humour (content). The article stresses that the term 'deadpan' actually 'refers only to the method of delivery.' Use this as a rule when analyzing or composing material: you can deliver lowbrow or highbrow content deadpan, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and role suitability (who benefits from deadpan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain character types and roles naturally suit deadpan delivery — for example, frustrated figures, authority figures, or straight men who deliver absurd lines with little expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John Cleese as Basil Fawlty (frustrated figure), Rowan Atkinson as authority figures (priests) speaking absurd lines, and many ensemble sitcom casts who emphasize deadpan delivery. Use deadpan for characters whose lack of expressive reaction heightens the humour of their statements or situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling and study of exemplary performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn deadpan by studying canonical performers and works noted for effective deadpan delivery (e.g., Buster Keaton, the 1928 Vitaphone short The Beau Brummels, Airplane!, Leslie Nielsen, Bill Murray, Bob Newhart, Monty Python, Steven Wright, Peter Sellers, Peter Cook & Dudley Moore, Ricky Gervais, Sacha Baron Cohen, Flight of the Conchords).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples as templates for facial control, timing, line understatement, and interaction with absurd contexts. The page lists many film and TV examples across eras and national traditions (British and American) as sources of technique and inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common confusions and distinctions (anti-humour and dry humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadpan is 'not to be confused with Anti-humor.' Dry humour is often confused with highbrow humour because the humour in dry humour requires seeing contradiction between words, delivery, and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or critiquing, explicitly distinguish deadpan delivery from anti-humour and from content-classifications; clarify whether a perceived failure is in delivery (deadpan execution) or in the comedic premise/context (content).
